comment.value:
We thank the reviewer for their thoughtful engagement and feedback. We agree that MimeQA invites more creative approaches to multimodal understanding. As the reviewer suggests, we further explore whether incorporating human body pose information could improve video LLMs’ performance on MimeQA.

We selected a 30% subset of MimeQA and applied PoseC3D [1], a skeleton-based action recognition model trained on NTU RGB+D [2], to generate action predictions every 10 seconds, selecting from a predefined set of 60 categories. We used HRnet to extract human body skeletons from raw videos [3], and we retained only action predictions with confidence scores above 60%. We chose the 60% threshold arbitrarily after manually checking a sample of the recognition results.  These timestamped labels were then included as additional input to the evaluation prompt of a Qwen2.5-VL-72B model. The prompt explicitly noted that the action recognition results might be helpful but potentially unreliable.

We found that the Qwen model with action recognition input achieved an overall accuracy of 16.16%, slightly below the base model's performance on the same video subset (16.84%). However, we observed marked improvements in specific categories that require fine-grained perceptual grounding, such as Grounding the Imagined (from 2.33% to 6.98%) and Working Memory (from 14.29% to 23.81%). Conversely, performance dropped in higher-level social reasoning categories, including Theory-of-Mind (from 52.17% to 34.78%) and Social Judgment (from 34.48% to 24.14%). We attribute these declines to hallucinations triggered by inaccurate or overly literal action labels. For example, a quarrel between actors is sometimes misclassified as “nausea or vomiting condition”, which misled the model during reasoning.

Notably, the improvement in Grounding the Imagined category was not achievable through other approaches explored in this paper, such as supervised fine-tuning. This suggests that integrating explicit pose-based perception modules are promising in addressing fundamental challenges in MimeQA. However, further work is needed to develop more nuanced integration strategies that preserve benefits for low-level grounding without compromising performance in high-level social reasoning tasks. We will include these discussions in the revised paper.

[1] Duan et al. “Revisiting skeleton-based action recognition.” CVPR. (2022).
[2] Shahroudy et al. “Ntu rgb+d: A large scale dataset for 3d human activity analysis.” CVPR. (2016).
[3] Sun et al. “Deep high-resolution representation learning for human pose estimation.” CVPR. (2019).

We thank the reviewer for their engagement and for acknowledging our response. We would like to further elaborate on the diversity of non-verbal human cues in MimeQA. As an additional analysis, we examined the reference answers for the “Grounding the Imagined” category and extracted all words ending in “-ing,” yielding a list of action-related terms. After removing mime- or performance-specific words (e.g., “pretending,” “portraying”), we obtained 68 unique action keywords – comparable to the range found in many action recognition datasets. To further estimate the diversity of physical actions portrayed in MimeQA, we ran PoseC3D [1], an action recognition model trained on the NTU RGB+D dataset [2], on 10-second clips from a 30% subset of MimeQA videos. Out of 60 possible action categories, the model identified 46 distinct actions across the subset. While this is only a proxy measure, we believe it reflects the broad range of perceived nonverbal behavior captured in MimeQA. 

We will include these discussions, along with word clouds of both the extracted action terms and the model recognition results, in the revised paper. We hope these additions help address the reviewer’s concerns about the diversity of our dataset.

[1] Duan et al. “Revisiting skeleton-based action recognition.” CVPR. (2022).

[2] Shahroudy et al. “Ntu rgb+d: A large scale dataset for 3d human activity analysis.” CVPR. (2016).

rebuttal.value:
We thank the reviewer for their thoughtful feedback and comments. Below we respond to the concerns raised by the reviewer.

> My major concern lies in the video sources. As mime videos are significantly different from natural videos (also significantly different from the pretraining datasets of existing large video-language models), without providing enough information or context, large video-language models will inevitably misinterpret the actions in the video. As also shown in the paper, providing some text information (Table 3) or simply the video title (Table 4) can significantly increase the performance. The great domain gap that exists in the dataset raises concern about the reliability of the evaluation of social intelligence.

We acknowledge the possibility that models may fail to grasp the task of mime understanding, for instance, by neglecting to infer the object being portrayed. To mitigate this, we included detailed context in the model prompt to clarify the task. For each model we benchmarked, we manually inspected 20 sampled responses on MimeQA to identify potential failures in mime comprehension (e.g., responses claiming the actor is not holding anything when the question asks for the portrayed invisible object). We found that none of the sampled responses (0%) exhibited such failures.

The fact that models trained on MimeQA transfers nicely to other social datasets, such as Social-IQ, also indicates the reliability and richness of mimes as a source of nonverbal human understanding (Section 4.2.2). As noted in the paper (Section 2). Mimes have been extensively used to evaluate humans’ social intelligence in fields of psychology and cognitive development. The use of pantomimic gestures also occurs in everyday life, for example, when a foreigner tries to ask the locals for directions without knowing their language. The ability of mime interpretation is also important in understanding individuals on the autism spectrum, who often extensively use body language to communicate.

Towards that end, the domain gap between MimeQA and existing social video datasets is a feature that helps to evaluate the true nonverbal understanding capabilities of models, not a bug. It enables a more rigorous assessment of models’ true nonverbal reasoning capabilities. Unlike prior benchmarks that often rely on verbal cues, subtitles, or background context that models may exploit, MimeQA’s purely nonverbal format demands that models infer meaning solely from human actions and visual context. This leads to fundamentally new challenges for foundation models. The purely nonverbal nature of mimes presents stronger stress tests on foundation models, requiring them to extract as much information as possible from visual cues and human actions alone – something that existing social datasets rarely demand. Therefore, MimeQA and existing, verbal-rich social datasets are complementary, and both are crucial for true multimodal social understanding.

It is also expected, then, that by providing the video context, such as the title, that the models should’ve inferred themselves, we obtain better accuracy. As an example, in a mime performance about a cricket game, providing the title “cricket” would greatly help the model to ground their responses, but humans can nonetheless infer that the actors are playing some bat game solely based on the humans’ gestures. Therefore, the increased performance with extra textual context is a failure mode of the current models’ reliance on text information rather than inferring from visual cues, not a concern about our dataset.

 

> Can authors provide more analysis on why fine-tuning on Social-IQ 2.0 can not improve the performance on the MIMEQA? As most large video-language models can not utilize audio information, training on Social-IQ 2.0 can also obtain the knowledge of nonverbal social intelligence. Is it simply due to the domain gap between the two datasets? Please also provide comparisons between MIMEQA, Social-IQ 2.0 and IntentQA.

We acknowledge that our fine-tuning of video-language models did not utilize audio information. However, in the presence of language and dialogues, real-world videos often do not contain as expressive of body language as mime performances do. We observe that, by fine-tuning on Social-IQ, the Qwen model did see a noticeable improvement on theory-of-mind questions (21.1% to 27.56%) and intention (8.8% to 11.7%), suggesting that the model did learn some high-level nonverbal intention understanding from Social-IQ. This improvement is particularly apparent when the question itself includes some context description for grounding. For example, to the question “How would the driver who came from behind feel towards the driver in front of her?”, the fine-tuned model accurately answers “the driver who came from behind would feel frustrated and angry.” 

At the same time, the model did perform worse on categories requiring more accurate interpretation of the mime actions, such as temporal reasoning (9.1% to 7.0%) and working memory (17.0% to 14.2%). This is often caused by increased hallucination when the Social-IQ fine-tuned model tries to read body gestures without physical object grounding. For instance, for the question “Why did the person on the left lose what he was holding?”, while the model fine-tuned on MimeQA accurately answers that the person lost the object in a quarrel with another person, the Social-IQ fine-tuned model misinterprets the scene as a dance routine. Thus, our analysis suggests that the nonverbal information in Social-IQ is insufficient, and sometimes worsen performance, on MimeQA which demands stronger nonverbal human understanding.

To confirm the transferability and uniqueness of social information in MimeQA, as the reviewer recommends, we additionally include the IntentQA dataset, and run a five-fold cross validation to confirm the reliability of our results.We take the validation set of IntentQA as they have similar number of questions as MimeQA, and adapt it to open-ended QA using the correct answer choice. The below table summarizes the improvement over the base model achieved by finetuned Qwen-2.5-VL-7B  models on various test datasets. 

| | MimeQA Test | Social-IQ Test | IntentQA Test |
| :---------------- | :------: | ----: | ----: |
Finetuned on MimeQA |3.5% $\pm$ 3.1% | 1.2%$\pm$ 3.0% |   2.6%$\pm$ 1.6%
Finetuned on Social-IQ | 0.4% $\pm$ 2.3%|  1.0%$\pm$ 2.3% | N/A
Finetuned on IntentQA  | 1.1% $\pm$ 3.4%| N/A | 3.7% $\pm$ 1.2%

On MimeQA, a paired t-test suggests that models fine-tuned on MimeQA achieves significantly better (p<0.05) accuracy over those fine-tuned on Social-IQ and IntentQA, although the significance should be taken with caution due to small number of folds. On Social-IQ, model fine-tuned on MimeQA achieve 1.2% $\pm$ 3.0% improvement, comparable to fine-tuning on Social-IQ (1.0% $\pm$ 2.3%). Similarly, on IntentQA, fine-tuning on MimeQA achieves 2.6% $\pm$ 1.6% improvement, comparable but slightly lower than fine-tuning on IntentQA (3.7% $\pm$ 1.2%). Overall, our results demonstrate that fine-tuning on MimeQA yields consistent and transferable gains across diverse social reasoning benchmarks, highlighting its unique contribution of social information not captured by existing datasets.

 

> Using vLLM as an abbreviation for video large language models will cause confusion, as vLLM is a well-known package for LLM inference-time acceleration.

We thank the reviewer for bringing this to our attention. We will address the abbreviation confusion in the final version of our paper.

> The question generation is done manually and essentially by two people. It is unclear if this is a good idea, it might lead to a narrow set of questions. It is unclear how well the diversity can be enforced.

We ensure the diversity of MimeQA through our carefully designed question hierarchy, which covers diverse social intelligence aspects across different temporal scales, from low-level action recognition to high-level theory-of-mind. Importantly, the abstract nature of mime performances may cause diverging interpretations and render questions unanswerable. Thus, we devote more human effort into quality checks by having a larger pool of human verifiers (4 in total) to ensure the answerability and quality of our annotations. Our benchmark is purposely designed to cover diverse aspects of social intelligence, and this is reflected in the even distribution of our question categories. 

 

> It would be interesting to see some baselines which have body-pose as an explicit input, and similarly some emotion recognition model to augment the VLM input (no training, just off-the shelf models).

We acknowledge that our dataset, as shown in our error analysis, demands more creative approaches to improve beyond current video language models. However, we want to keep the focus of the paper on introducing a novel task in multimodal social understanding, and evaluate the capability of currently best pretrained LVLMs, as the current prevailing paradigm is that LVLMs have general reasoning capabilities which we rigorously evaluated for nonverbal social intelligence in our paper, including model prompting and fine-tuning. The uniqueness and creative nature of our task meant that there is no established approach, and we encourage future approaches towards foundation models with truly multimodal social reasoning.

 

> Some of the questions on scene-level understanding don't require video understanding, just requires correct frame to be chosen which might make it less interesting in certain cases.

While scene-level questions generally require only a small segment of the entire video, they still require video understanding on, for example, the characters’ sentiments and cause-and-effect reasoning. One example is a question, “Why did the man on the right leave the table?”, for a video where the actor on the left exhibits poor table manners in a restaurant, causing the man the right to leave. Answering the question requires the model to identify and aggregate various pieces of evidence across the short scene, such as understanding the sentiment of the man leaving, the actions of the man at the table, and expected social norms. These questions are still highly interesting, as they require sufficient understanding of the scene’s social context, combining visual cues with commonsense knowledge. Our datasets incorporate questions on various temporal scales, from frame-level action recognition to whole-video social reasoning, to holistically evaluate models’ social understanding in video comprehension settings.

 

>  Since evaluation is via LLM-as-Judge, it can be expensive to run, though it might be a good thing since the idea is to see generalization and not run repeated evals.

We acknowledge the potential drawbacks and biases of LLM judges. However, we note that in practice, the cost is relatively inexpensive as the input to the LLM judge are text tokens. Assuming that the input prompt and output of the judge is on average 200 tokens and 100 tokens respectively per question, the total input tokens is ~160k and the total output tokens is ~80k. Using the current input and output costs for GPT-4o, which are $2.50 per 1m tokens for input and $10.00 per 1m tokens for output, the total estimated cost is $1.21 to evaluate a model’s responses over the full dataset.. Additionally, while we decided to create an open-ended question-answering task, we can extend our benchmark to be formatted as multiple choice QA through semi-automatic pipelines for answer decoy generation . We choose open-ended question answering to help mitigate biases in question and answer choices.

 

>  Authors should also include recent reasoning VLM models such as o3 or gemini-2.5pro baselines.

We additionally benchmark Gemini-2.5-pro and GPT-o3 on MimeQA, and we report the results below.

||Overall Accuracy|
| :------------- | :------: | 
|Gemini-2.5-pro| 38.3%|
|GPT-o3| 34.4%|
|Human| **86.0%**|

**Under Limitations Weaknesses**

> The paper misses relevant work like the Mimetics Dataset; Weinzaepfel et al which also studies human action understanding in mime videos.

We thank the reviewer for bringing our attention to the Mimetics dataset, and we will include it in the related works. The Mimetics dataset is an action classification dataset that uses short video clips of “out-of-context” human actions to robustly evaluate action recognition. In contrast, our MimeQA dataset uses mime performances, which have been extensively used to evaluate human intelligence (see section 2 for discussion), to holistically evaluate models’ nonverbal social intelligence. Although the Mimetics could be seen as a supplement to our “Grounding the Imagined” question category, our work serves as a benchmark for broader social intelligence, which encompasses not just action recognition but also a diverse set of question categories, including questions pertaining to understanding human emotions, social norms, and theory of mind. By framing our tasks as open-ended question answering, MimeQA is a much more realistic test of social intelligence that captures the nuances of body language sequences. Furthermore, while Mimetics questions are answerable with 1-10 sec clips, MimeQA’s questions require the model to reason over extended periods of time, as the videos range from 1-10 min long (Figure 4). Therefore, our dataset makes a unique contribution by providing high-quality annotations to facilitate advanced nonverbal social reasoning for today’s multimodal foundation models.

 

> The dataset consists of 221 videos with 806 total questions which seems small to cover a diverse range that humans display. The 221 videos seem smaller than 713 video clips in the Mimetics dataset from 2019.

As mentioned above, the Mimetics dataset consists of short video clips, ranging from 1 to 10 seconds. In contrast, MimeQA consists of videos from 1 to 10 minutes, covering a complete story plot conveyed through various human gestures. Thus, the total video time of MimeQA videos is 8 hours, whereas the clips in the Mimetics dataset is at most 10 seconds long, so an upper bound on the total video time is 713 * 10 sec = 2 hours. Furthermore, each video in MimeQA contains a wider range of human action than isolated video clips in Mimetics, and our diverse question categories evaluate more aspects of social intelligence.

 

> Details about the methodology used to create the dataset is missing. Did the authors consider leveraging existing datasets such as Kinetics to source keywords.

We used a set of generic keywords related to mime, such as "mime performance","mime show”, "mime act", etc. .to collect videos from YouTube. We will include the full list of keywords in the paper’s appendix. Our collection process yields a much broader range of social settings, beyond localized actions. As the purpose of our benchmark is to test general social understanding across a story plot, we are unable to directly use action labels, which only identify isolated video clips.

> a) Only two human annotators were used to generate questions for each video. This might result in reduced diversity.

We ensure the diversity of MimeQA through our carefully designed question hierarchy, which covers diverse social intelligence aspects across different temporal scales, from low-level action recognition to high-level theory-of-mind. Importantly, the abstract nature of mime performances may cause diverging interpretations and render questions unanswerable. Our benchmark is purposely designed to cover diverse aspects of social intelligence, and this is reflected in the even distribution of our question categories. 

> b) As mentioned in the limitations, these videos are likely to be from Western countries further reducing the breadth of concepts that the benchmark tests.

We acknowledge that the interpretation of mime performances, though effective in cross-cultural settings, may still be influenced by cultural context and perceived gender of the performer. To understand the cultural and demographic biases in MimeQA, we randomly sampled 25% of the videos in the dataset and manually annotated two attributes using both the video content and its title/description: (1) whether the cultural context appeared Western or non-Western, and (2) the perceived binary genders (male/female) of the individuals depicted. Our analysis indicates that 56% of the sampled videos reflect non-Western cultural contexts, with many sources originating from Asian regions. In terms of gender, 88% of videos feature at least one male participant, and 68% include at least one female participant. A majority of videos contain both male and female participants. Thus, although MimeQA was not explicitly curated to enforce cultural or gender diversity, these findings suggest a reasonably balanced representation across both dimensions, with no dominant cultural or gender skew.

 

> The paper presents analysis on finetuning the models (in table 2) on 80% of the dataset and testing on the remaining 20% (~161 questions). With 92% alignment between automated grader and human, are the results statistically significant? Did the authors do cross-validation to measure the variance?

To show the reliability of our finetuning results (table 2), we run a five-fold cross validation and report the results below. 
|Model | MimeQA Test Accuracy|
| :---------------- | :------: | 
| Finetuned on MimeQA | **25.1% $\pm$ 2.0%**|
| Base |  21.6% $\pm$ 2.2% |

We observe that, on average, the base Qwen model achieves an accuracy of 21.6% $\pm$ 2.2% on MimeQA, while the model fine-tuned on MimeQA achieves an accuracy of 25.1% $\pm$ 2.0% accuracy. A paired t-test yields a p-value of 0.06, narrowly missing the conventional threshold for statistical significance. However, the consistent improvement across all folds and the low variance in results strongly suggest that the fine-tuned model outperforms the base model in a meaningful way. Given the limited number of folds, the p-value likely underestimates the true significance of the observed gains.

We additionally run a five-fold cross validation on our transfer experiments (figure 5). We observe that, on MimeQA, Qwen models fine-tuned on MimeQA achieve an average of 3.5% $\pm$ 3.1% improvement, whereas finetuning on Social-IQ only results in an average of 0.4% $\pm$ 2.3% improvement over the base model. The improvement achieved by the model fine-tuned on MimeQA on Social-IQ is statistically significant (p=0.02), whereas the improvement for the model fine-tuned on Social-IQ is not (p>0.1). Meanwhile, finetuning on MimeQA exhibited an improvement of (1.2% $\pm$ 3.0%) when transferred to  Social-IQ, which is comparable to the improvement attained by directly fine-tuning on Social-IQ (1.0% $\pm$ 2.3%).

 

> Did the authors conduct extensive prompt engineering to measure the impact of the prompt? Will techniques like chain-of-thought, etc improve performance?

We have designed our prompt to ensure that VLMs understand the context of mime performances, rather than interpreting the performances as natural scenes. Additionally, we experiment with chain-of-thought prompting. Below are the results:
|Model |Without CoT| With CoT|
| :---------------- | :------: |  :------: | 
|Qwen-2.5VL |20.1%|**22.2%**|
|LLaVA-Video | **19.4%**|17.7%|
|InternV2.5L| **21.6%**|18.7%|
|VideoLLaMA3|**22.2%**| 17.7%|
|GPT-4o|**31.3%** |29.5%|

For example, we find that GPT-4o with CoT tends to hallucinate more for the “Grounding the Imagined,” “Temporal Reasoning,” and “Affect Recognition” categories. This finding is in line with prior work [1] that shows CoT is not always helpful for tasks which lack symbolic reasoning. We will add these results to our revised paper.

summary.value:
The paper introduces MimeQA, a new benchmark dataset designed to evaluate the nonverbal social intelligence of video-language models (vLLMs) using mime performances, i.e., videos that rely solely on gesture and body language without spoken words.
The authors curated 806 carefully annotated question-answer pairs across 101 videos to assess grounding (e.g., recognizing imagined objects), scene-level understanding (e.g., emotional or intentional inference), and global reasoning (e.g., theory of mind, social judgment). State-of-the-art models, including GPT-4o and Gemini 1.5, achieved 20–30% accuracy below the human baseline of 86%, highlighting limitations in current vLLMs' understanding of nonverbal cues.

strengths_contributions.value:
* The paper fills a gap by addressing nonverbal social reasoning, an underexplored area in multimodal AI. The benchmark may inspire improvements in multimodal social reasoning, especially in non-verbal human cues.
* The dataset is carefully curated, annotated, and verified, with a strong emphasis on annotation quality and question diversity across cognitive levels.
* The authors benchmark both closed- and open-source models, perform fine-tuning experiments, conduct transfer learning studies, and present insightful error analyses that reveal systemic weaknesses in vLLMs.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
* While rich in quality, the dataset comprises only 8 hours of video and 806 QA pairs, which may restrict generalization and scalability for training large models.
* The mime videos and their annotations may reflect primarily Western social norms, potentially limiting cross-cultural applicability. The variation in mimes should differ depending on the culture.

summary.value: Brief Summary: The paper proposes the task of video qa but on mime videos (~8 hrs) sourced from youtube videos. The key insight is that mime performances are purely visual and require VLMs to have an accurate understanding of body movements and correspond it to a social setting. The authors follow structured construction pipeline of fetch, annotate and verify with the questions having hierarchical structure spanning scene-level and global-level understanding. This results in 806 total questions.

strengths_contributions.value:
Pros:

1. It is a very interesting and unique idea to be honest. I think mime videos can serve as a very good frame of reference for social intelligence of VLMs. 

2. The authors have done all the sensible things such as verifying annotation agreement, and the LLM-as-Judge is verified to have agreement of 92% with human. 

3. The dataset is essentially unsolved with gpt-4o getting 31.3% points far behind human accuracy of 86%, which suggests there is scope for improvement for VLMs.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
Cons:

1. The question generation is done manually and essentially by two people. It is unclear if this is a good idea, it might lead to a narrow set of questions. It is unclear how well the diversity can be enforced. 

2. It would be interesting to see some baselines which have body-pose as an explicit input, and similarly some emotion recognition model to augment the VLM input (no training, just off-the shelf models). 

3. Some of the questions on scene-level understanding don't require video understanding, just requires correct frame to be chosen which might make it less interesting in certain cases.

1. (Minor) Since evaluation is via LLM-as-Judge, it can be expensive to run, though it might be a good thing since the idea is to see generalization and not run repeated evals. 

1. (Minor) Authors should also include recent reasoning VLM models such as o3 or gemini-2.5pro baselines.

dataset_code_comments.value: The dataset is available to be used from huggingface directly

final_justification.value: I was already positive on the paper, and given that even leading models such as gemini-2.5-pro and o3 struggle in this benchmark is a very good sign that the dataset isn't saturated yet.

summary.value: This paper focuses on nonverbal social communication and collect a dataset based on mime videos. Actors in mime videos express their feelings and intentions based on exaggerated facial expressions and body language, posing great challenges to recent large video-language models for understanding. The dataset is collected and annotated based on rigorous standards, ensuring high quality. The paper also provides detailed error analysis, providing a deeper understanding on the unique characteristics and challenges of this dataset.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. The paper focuses on a significant and valuable ability of video-language models, ie nonverbal social communication. It could greatly advance the understanding of human behavior and benefit human-agent interaction.
2. The collected dataset is high-quality. The question and the answer are generated by human annotators and further checked by another human annotator. The preference from humans is also in line with the understanding of nonverbal social communication with humans.
3. The error analysis is detailed and insightful. Finetuning on other datasets can not improve the performance on MimeQA, demonstrating its distinctive characteristic, ie nonverbal social intelligence. Error analysis shows that improving models in interpreting imagined objects and nuanced understanding of social signals could improve the ability of nonverbal social intelligence.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. My major concern lies in the video sources. As mime videos are significantly different from natural videos (also significantly different from the pretraining datasets of existing large video-language models), without providing enough information or context, large video-language models will inevitably misinterpret the actions in the video. As also shown in the paper, providing some text information (Table 3) or simply the video title (Table 4) can significantly increase the performance. The great domain gap that exists in the dataset raises concern about the reliability of the evaluation of social intelligence.
2. Can authors provide more analysis on why fine-tuning on Social-IQ 2.0 can not improve the performance on the MIMEQA? As most large video-language models can not utilize audio information, training on Social-IQ 2.0 can also obtain the knowledge of nonverbal social intelligence.  Is it simply due to the domain gap between the two datasets? Please also provide comparisons between MIMEQA, Social-IQ 2.0 and IntentQA.
3. (minor issue) Using vLLM as an abbreviation for video large language models will cause confusion, as vLLM is a well-known package for LLM inference-time acceleration.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

final_justification.value: Thanks for the rebuttal from authors. After reading the rebuttal, I acknowledge the value of the benchmark and the unique characteristics of the nonverbal social intelligence which is different from other benchmarks that rely on verbal cues, subtitles, or background context. I agree with authors on that MineQA are complementary with other verbal-rich social datasets. Thus, I will raise the rating to borderline accept.

title.value: MimeQA: Towards Socially-Intelligent Nonverbal Foundation Models

abstract.value: As AI becomes more closely integrated with peoples' daily activities, socially intelligent AI that can understand and interact seamlessly with humans in daily lives is increasingly important. However, current works in AI social reasoning all rely on language-only or language-dominant approaches to benchmark and training models, resulting in systems that are improving in verbal communication but struggle with nonverbal social understanding. To address this limitation, we tap into a novel data source rich in nonverbal social interactions -- mime videos. Mimes refer to the art of expression through gesture and movement without spoken words, which presents unique challenges and opportunities in interpreting nonverbal social communication. We contribute a new dataset called MimeQA, obtained by sourcing ~8 hours of videos clips from YouTube and developing a comprehensive video question-answering benchmark comprising 806 carefully annotated and verified question-answer pairs, designed to probe nonverbal social reasoning capabilities. Using MimeQA, we evaluate state-of-the-art video large language models (VideoLLMs) and find that they achieve low accuracy, generally ranging from 20-30%, while humans score 86\%. Our analysis reveals that VideoLLMs often fail to ground imagined objects and over-rely on the text prompt while ignoring subtle nonverbal interactions. We hope to inspire future work in AI models that embody true social intelligence capable of interpreting non-verbal human interactions.
